PHẦN A: 1. Astronomers believe that studying the cosmos helps us understand our own origins as well as the origins of everything around us. — "cosmos" luôn dùng ở số ít, chỉ vũ trụ như một tổng thể có trật tự; hay đi với "explore/study the cosmos". 2. Some scientists speculate that extraterrestrial life could exist in environments we once assumed were entirely uninhabitable. — tính từ "extraterrestrial" (ngoài Trái Đất) thường đi trước "life/beings"; phân biệt với "international". 3. Many experts argue that any serious attempt to colonise another planet would require decades of preparation and international cooperation. — chú ý chính tả Anh-Anh "colonise" (không phải "colonize"); hay đi với "colonise Mars/a planet". 4. The surface of Mars is often described as inhospitable because of its thin atmosphere and extreme temperature swings. — "inhospitable" mô tả môi trường khắc nghiệt, không phù hợp sinh sống; hay đi với "environment/conditions/climate". 5. Astronauts have to adapt quickly to weightlessness once their spacecraft reaches orbit. — danh từ chỉ trạng thái không trọng lượng; hay đi với "experience/a state of weightlessness". 6. The cost of building and launching a new generation of space telescopes is widely considered prohibitive for most national space agencies acting alone. — "prohibitive" (quá đắt đỏ, ngăn cản) khác với "prohibited" (bị cấm); hay đi với "prohibitive cost/price tag". 7. Robotic probes have been sent to explore the outer planets because sending humans there remains far beyond current technology. — danh từ "probe" chỉ tàu thăm dò không người lái; hay đi với "launch a probe/an interplanetary probe". 8. Mission engineers must calculate a spacecraft's trajectory with extreme precision so that it reaches its intended destination. — "trajectory" là đường bay/quỹ đạo của vật thể, khác với "orbit" (quỹ đạo khép kín quanh một thiên thể). 9. Researchers are still debating how many exoplanets might actually be habitable once we account for factors such as radiation and atmospheric composition. — "habitable" (có thể sống được) hay đi với "a habitable planet/zone"; trái nghĩa là "uninhabitable". 10. The distances between stars are so vast that even our fastest spacecraft would take an astronomical amount of time to reach the nearest one. — "astronomical" ở đây mang nghĩa "khổng lồ, khó tưởng tượng", khác với nghĩa gốc "thuộc thiên văn học". 11. Engineers continue to grapple with the challenge of shielding astronauts from cosmic radiation during long-duration missions. — cụm động từ luôn đi kèm giới từ "with", nghĩa là vật lộn/cố gắng giải quyết một vấn đề khó. 12. The discovery of a new exoplanet orbiting a distant star often reignites public interest in the search for life beyond our solar system. — "exoplanet" viết liền một từ, chỉ hành tinh ngoài hệ Mặt Trời.

passages.text: Low Earth orbit, a band of space extending from roughly 200 to 2,000 kilometres above the surface, has become, within a decade, one of the most rapidly transformed environments in the recent history of resource use. The principal driver has been the deployment of so-called mega-constellations: networks of several thousand small communications satellites that operate in coordinated formation. The first commercial system of this kind exceeded 1,000 active spacecraft in 2020; by 2024, a single operator was managing more than 6,000, and three additional constellations of comparable scale had been authorised. The pace of change has overtaken the international regime designed to regulate orbital activity, and the resulting tensions are now the subject of active debate among aerospace engineers, economists and treaty specialists.

The technical case for mega-constellations rests primarily on latency and coverage. Professor Mariko Eguchi, an aerospace systems engineer at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, has argued that low-orbit networks can deliver internet connectivity to communities that geostationary satellites, positioned at 36,000 kilometres altitude, cannot economically reach. Her group's analysis indicates that the round-trip signal delay falls from approximately 600 milliseconds in geostationary systems to under 40 milliseconds in low-orbit constellations, a difference that is critical for applications such as remote surgery and high-frequency financial trading. Eguchi concedes that the proliferation of small satellites raises significant collision risks, but she argues that the technical benefits are sufficiently substantial to warrant continued deployment, provided that adequate end-of-life disposal protocols can be enforced.

A more critical reading has been offered by Dr Thandiwe Mokoena, an orbital debris specialist at the South African National Space Agency. Mokoena's team has modelled the cumulative effect of multiple overlapping constellations and concluded that, even with conservative disposal compliance rates, the resulting fragment population may exceed the carrying capacity of certain altitude bands within two decades. She has drawn particular attention to the so-called Kessler cascade, a self-sustaining sequence in which collisions among existing fragments generate further fragments, each of which becomes a potential collider in its turn. Mokoena does not advocate halting deployment, but she argues that current regulatory frameworks substantially underestimate the time horizon over which fragment populations remain hazardous.

The economic dimension has been examined by Dr Aleksey Petrov, a space economist at the European University Institute in Florence. Petrov has noted that the costs of orbital debris are externalised: a satellite operator pays for its own launch and operations but typically faces no proportional charge for the long-term hazard its spacecraft impose on subsequent users of the same orbital band. Petrov's group has proposed a system of orbital use fees, calibrated to the predicted debris footprint of each mission, on the model of carbon pricing in atmospheric policy. He acknowledges that such a scheme would require multilateral agreement at the level of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and that historical progress in that forum has been slow.

A further area of contention concerns active debris removal, the use of dedicated spacecraft to capture and de-orbit existing fragments. Trials by the European Space Agency, including the ClearSpace-1 mission scheduled for late 2026, are designed to demonstrate that fragments larger than ten centimetres can be retrieved using robotic arms and controlled re-entry burns. Critics of the approach, including Professor Connor Whitford, an aerospace policy researcher at the University of Edinburgh, argue that the unit cost of active removal remains prohibitive when set against the millions of small fragments below the tracking threshold. Whitford does not dismiss the trials, but he argues that prevention through stricter launch licensing and mandatory disposal manoeuvres is likely to yield better outcomes per dollar spent than retrospective cleanup.

The political picture is complicated by competing national interests. Established space-faring states with substantial commercial operators tend to favour voluntary codes of conduct, while states with limited current operations have generally pressed for binding international standards that would constrain future market entry by larger players. Dr Ananya Iyer, a science-policy analyst at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, has observed that this asymmetry has produced a negotiating impasse: the very actors whose cooperation is most necessary for an effective regime are those with the strongest commercial incentive to delay it. Iyer is careful to add that this account is not a simple morality tale, since some commercial operators have voluntarily exceeded current disposal requirements, partly because in-orbit collisions threaten their own assets.

The most tenable view, given what is currently known, treats orbital governance as pressing yet resistant to any single dramatic fix. The technical benefits of mega-constellations are real, and the network effects on global connectivity are unlikely to be reversed. The hazards of unchecked debris generation are also real, and the time horizons over which they materialise extend well beyond the political cycles in which current decisions are taken. The more searching question, by this writer’s reading, is whether economic instruments such as orbital use fees, combined with stricter licensing and selective active removal, can buy enough time for international coordination to catch up with the underlying technology. On the available evidence, that catching-up remains possible but is not assured.

audio_scripts.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture closes our orbital environment series — turning from launch economics to what is increasingly the binding constraint on low-Earth-orbit operations: the cumulative population of human-made debris. [pause:5s] The conceptual frame I'll draw on comes from the work of Professor Mikael Olusegun-Brandt — that's O-L-U-S-E-G-U-N hyphen B-R-A-N-D-T, no umlaut, silent T at the end of Brandt. Olusegun-Brandt's 2016 review reframed orbital debris from a launch-by-launch nuisance into what he calls "self-sustaining collisional cascade theory". [pause:3s] First, some historical orientation. The orbital-population dataset I'll quote was first archived in 2005 — sorry, let me correct that, 2003; the descriptive synthesis was published in 2005 but the catalogue itself was assembled from 2003. So whenever I reference the catalogue baseline, please record 2003. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation. Olusegun-Brandt's cascade USED TO be tracked using ground radar alone — quite limited above one thousand kilometres — NOW the field combines ground radar with on-orbit optical sensors and laser-ranging stations, and from 2027 a multinational consortium WILL be rolling out continuous space-based debris-track telescopes. So past, present, future. For today's session I'm focusing on the CURRENT tracking regime — that is, the ground-plus-on-orbit pairing. Moving to terminology. The runaway collision phenomenon Olusegun-Brandt foregrounds — where each debris-producing collision generates fragments that go on to cause further collisions, escalating debris density without further launches — is termed the "Kessler syndrome". Now, you'll see related labels in the older literature: collisional avalanche, fragment chain reaction, runaway orbital fouling. All gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Olusegun-Brandt's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is the Kessler syndrome — K-E-S-S-L-E-R syndrome. So when the older corpus uses collisional avalanche or fragment chain reaction, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to flag is what orbital mechanics call the "altitude residence cascade". When debris analysts describe how long different objects remain in orbit before atmospheric drag pulls them down, they sketch a graded cascade running from short-residence very-low-Earth altitudes through decade-residence low-Earth altitudes to effectively-permanent geostationary altitudes. So, you know, you'll find a paint flake at three hundred kilometres burning up in a few years — that's short residence. Or an upper-stage tank at twelve hundred kilometres lingering for centuries — that's effectively-permanent residence. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical label. The umbrella term is the altitude residence cascade. [pause:3s] Now, the catalogue data — and please pay close attention because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the thirty-six thousand catalogued objects larger than ten centimetres in low-Earth orbit at last audit, MOST are non-functional fragments — roughly sixty-eight per cent. Only a few — about seven per cent — are currently active payloads, and some — twenty-five per cent — are spent rocket bodies or defunct payload hulks. So non-functional fragments dominate numerically, but the active-payload tail, though small, is operationally critical. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to introduce is "post-mission disposal". This refers to the planned end-of-life manoeuvre by which an active satellite is either deorbited into the atmosphere or pushed to a graveyard orbit, rather than left as future debris. At the Delft tracking facility our team logged eighty-four documented compliant disposals across one calendar year. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that simply launching fewer missions reduces collision risk in a linear way is, frankly, not supported. Most of the cascade simulations in our dataset did NOT show the predicted monotonic decline in collision rate when launch cadence was halved. Quite the opposite — many showed a non-linear plateau, because legacy debris dominates even after launches drop. So the older "fewer-launches-is-enough" hypothesis, which predicts proportional debris reduction, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I opened with. That CURRENT ground-plus-on-orbit tracking state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in next week's tutorial. I want you to focus on the optical-sensor tasking protocols specifically, not the space-based telescope futures or the legacy radar-only instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: low-Earth-orbit debris is governed by a Kessler-syndrome cascade, not launch volume alone; non-functional fragments dominate the catalogue at roughly sixty-eight per cent; the fewer-launches-is-enough hypothesis is not empirically supported; and post-mission disposal compliance is the operational lever we control. Next week we'll examine active debris removal. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The two bar charts present satellite-launch activity by sector in 2023 and the cumulative volume of tracked orbital debris at selected years between 2000 and 2023.

Overall, the commercial sector overwhelmingly dominated launch activity, far outstripping government and military missions, while the amount of orbital debris rose throughout the period, with the sharpest increase occurring most recently.

Turning first to launches, commercial operators conducted by far the most missions, at roughly 2,400 in 2023. By comparison, government and military launches were modest and broadly comparable, at 90 and 60 respectively. The commercial figure therefore dwarfed the other two sectors combined, reflecting the rise of large commercial mega-constellations.

The debris panel shows a clear upward trend. The number of tracked objects climbed steadily from 9,000 in 2000 to 16,000 in 2010 and 23,000 by 2020, before rising steeply to 36,000 in 2023. The steepest jump thus occurred in the final three years. This pattern suggests that the surge in commercial launches coincided with a marked acceleration in orbital debris, raising clear concerns about space sustainability in low Earth orbit.

The two public sectors remained modest and broadly comparable, underscoring how decisively private mega-constellations now drive access to orbit.

Tracked objects rose gently from 9,000 in 2000 to 16,000 in 2010, then to 23,000 by 2020, before surging to 36,000 in 2023; well over a third of the total accumulation thus occurred in just the final three years. What the juxtaposition implies is that the explosion in commercial launches has coincided with a pronounced acceleration in residual debris — a correlation that casts serious doubt on the long-term sustainability of low Earth orbit, even if causation cannot be established from the data alone.

blocks.text: Public investment in the cosmic frontier has historically generated a cascade of spin-off technologies, from satellite navigation to medical imaging, that now underpin everyday life.
Earth-observation satellites deliver an indispensable vantage point for tracking deforestation, monitoring sea-level rise and forecasting extreme weather.
Planetary defence initiatives designed to detect and deflect hazardous asteroids function as a form of civilisational insurance that few other fields of research can offer.
Sustained funding for fundamental astrophysics has repeatedly yielded awe-inspiring discoveries that expand humanity's grasp of the cosmos far beyond practical application alone.
Crewed missions to colonise distant worlds remain prohibitive, often running into hundreds of billions of dollars for a single undertaking.
The astronomical sums allocated to flagship programmes are, critics argue, a misallocation of capital in a world still riddled with entrenched poverty.
Accumulating space debris in low Earth orbit threatens to render vital satellite infrastructure unusable, jeopardising communications and navigation services on which modern economies depend.
Suborbital space tourism delivers scant scientific return while conspicuously widening the gap in visible privilege between wealthy passengers and those struggling with basic needs on the ground.
The privatisation of spaceflight, spearheaded by ambitious entrepreneurs, has driven down launch costs and reopened a frontier once monopolised by national space agencies.
Growing scientific curiosity about whether extraterrestrial life exists beyond our solar system continues to justify substantial expenditure on deep-space probes.
Geopolitical rivalry between major powers has historically been a potent driver of ambitious space programmes, much as it was during the original space race.
The discovery of thousands of confirmed exoplanets, some orbiting within a star's Goldilocks zone, has reignited public fascination with the search for habitable worlds.
Should orbital collisions cascade unchecked, the resulting Kessler syndrome scenario could leave near-Earth space effectively unusable for generations.
Breakthroughs originally developed for trajectory calculation and spacecraft navigation have filtered down into industries as varied as aviation and logistics.
Prolonged weightlessness during extended missions inflicts measurable physiological harm on astronauts, including significant bone density loss.
Heightened public awareness of planetary defence has, over time, fostered greater international cooperation on tracking near-Earth objects.
Engineers must continually grapple with the challenge of shielding crews from cosmic radiation during long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit.
Assessing a planet's genuine habitability is far more complex than merely confirming that it lies within a star's Goldilocks zone; a full habitability index requires numerous additional variables.
Coordinating an increasingly crowded orbital environment, cluttered with defunct satellites and fragments, poses a persistent challenge for regulators and private operators alike.
Reconciling the prohibitive cost of crewed exploration with pressing terrestrial needs remains one of the most contentious policy dilemmas of our time.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: International treaties could mandate the responsible de-orbiting of defunct satellites to prevent the space debris problem from escalating into a full-blown Kessler syndrome event.

Rather than treating the debate as binary, governments could disaggregate the budget, ring-fencing modest funding for planetary defence and Earth-observation while continuing humanitarian spending in parallel.
Expanding privatisation under strict regulatory oversight could keep launch costs falling without sacrificing safety standards or environmental accountability.
Investing in reusable rocket technology and in-orbit refuelling could gradually ease the astronomical costs that currently limit ambitious missions to a handful of well-funded nations.
Many members of the public still regard ambitions to colonise Mars as not rocket science in principle but staggeringly difficult in practice, given how genuinely inhospitable the Martian surface is.
A considerable segment of public opinion views crewed exploration as a false economy, arguing that the same funds could achieve far more if redirected towards poverty relief.
The notion that becoming a multi-planetary species offers long-term insurance against extinction has gained significant traction among scientists and policymakers alike.
Sceptics frequently dismiss the entire enterprise as a profligate vanity project pursued largely for the prestige of billionaires and governments.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: National space agencies bear primary responsibility for regulating orbital traffic and mitigating the space debris they themselves have generated over decades.
Private aerospace companies driving the privatisation of spaceflight must be held accountable for the environmental footprint of increasingly frequent rocket launches.
International bodies coordinating planetary defence need to establish binding protocols for detecting and responding to hazardous near-Earth objects before a crisis occurs.
Governments funding off-world colonisation research carry a duty to ensure that such spending does not come at the expense of essential domestic welfare programmes.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: Although crewed missions appear prohibitive, the actual share of global GDP devoted to space agencies is a vanishingly small fraction, hardly a plausible explanation for unresolved poverty.
While sceptics frame planetary exploration as profligate, advocates counter that the spin-off technologies it generates have already repaid the initial investment many times over.
It could be argued that suborbital space tourism, however elitist it may appear, is gradually democratising access to space as competition drives prices down.
Critics who dismiss the search for extraterrestrial life as frivolous overlook the fact that such research routinely advances fields as practical as robotics and materials science.
A growing number of national and private space actors are expected to pursue off-world colonisation projects, however distant such ambitions currently remain.
As detection technology matures, scientists anticipate refining the habitability index used to evaluate newly discovered exoplanets, narrowing the search for genuinely liveable worlds.
Continued privatisation is likely to keep driving launch costs down, potentially making orbital travel accessible to a wider segment of the population within coming decades.
International cooperation on planetary defence and orbital debris mitigation is projected to intensify as the risks of inaction become harder to ignore.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas the earliest missions were financed and operated exclusively by government agencies, today's cosmic frontier is increasingly shaped by private enterprise.
Unlike terrestrial environmental problems, which unfold gradually, a Kessler syndrome cascade could render orbital space unusable within a remarkably short span of time.

Compared with the fanciful, science-fiction image of instant terraforming, the reality of adapting an inhospitable planet like Mars for human habitation remains an immensely slower and more uncertain process.
In contrast to the astronomical sums spent on crewed exploration, robotic probes achieve much of the same scientific return at a fraction of the cost.
A well-documented case study of how satellite-derived climate data, gathered by Earth-observation satellites, has informed international environmental policy.
A hypothetical scenario illustrating how a Kessler syndrome cascade might unfold if orbital debris mitigation measures continue to be neglected.
Statements from scientists who hypothesise that liquid water may exist on certain moons in our solar system, cited to show ongoing interest in extraterrestrial life.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: Whether humanity should pour resources into venturing beyond our atmosphere or concentrate first on terrestrial problems has become a perennial debate. Both camps make legitimate points, but in my view the dichotomy is overstated.

Champions of space exploration argue that pushing the cosmic frontier yields outsized scientific dividends. The Apollo programme, for example, produced spin-off technologies ranging from satellite communications to medical imaging that we now take for granted. Earth-observation satellites, in particular, are indispensable for tracking deforestation, monitoring sea-level rise and forecasting hurricanes — much of what we know about climate change comes from looking back from orbit. Furthermore, given that an asteroid impact could one day threaten our species, planetary defence and off-world colonisation are arguably insurance policies for civilisation.

Critics, however, contend that such missions are profligate when measured against unmet earthly needs. The cost of a single crewed Mars mission is estimated to exceed a trillion dollars, a sum which could fund universal vaccination, primary education or hunger relief many times over. There is also a moral discomfort in watching billionaires fly to the edge of space for leisure while millions lack reliable sanitation. From this angle, space looks less like a frontier and more like a vanity project.

In my view, the choice is not binary. The actual share of global GDP devoted to space agencies is under 0.1 per cent — hardly a drain that explains away poverty. Space exploration and humanitarian spending can, and arguably must, advance in parallel. A balanced budget, rather than an either/or stance, seems the most sensible position.

Few policy debates polarise public opinion as sharply as whether humanity should commit serious resources to space exploration or focus its energies on alleviating earthbound suffering. Although both perspectives are intellectually defensible, I am persuaded that the supposed trade-off is largely illusory.

Advocates of an expansive space agenda point to a cascade of tangible returns that often go unnoticed. The miniaturisation of electronics, advances in materials science and the entire architecture of global positioning — without which modern logistics and precision agriculture would falter — all owe a debt to public investment in aerospace. Earth-observation constellations, moreover, are now the linchpin of climate monitoring, supplying real-time data on Arctic ice loss and biosphere health. Seldom, indeed, has so small a fraction of GDP delivered such outsized civilisational dividends.

Sceptics, by contrast, frame planetary exploration as a misallocation of capital in a world still riddled with destitution. Why, they ask, dispatch probes to the outer solar system when hundreds of millions subsist on a few dollars a day? Compounding this critique is the rise of suborbital space tourism, whose carbon-intensive launches deliver scant scientific value while widening the optics gap between billionaire passengers and the global poor. Such concerns command genuine moral weight.

The reconciliation, in my view, lies in disaggregating the budget. Allocating modest yet sustained funding to fundamental research, planetary defence and Earth-observation missions need not crowd out development aid; the two streams operate on entirely different fiscal scales. Crucially, the long-term insurance value of becoming a multi-planetary species cannot be priced in quarterly terms. Decoupling space from humanitarian commitment is, ultimately, a false economy, and a pluralist stance is preferable to either extreme.

B. CUE CARD + MODEL ANSWER

Model Answer (268 words):

The space mission that has captivated my imagination most profoundly is the James Webb Space Telescope - the long-awaited successor to Hubble, which was launched on Christmas Day 2021 and began returning its first full-colour scientific images in July 2022.

I first encountered Webb's imagery somewhat serendipitously while scrolling through Twitter that summer. The unveiling of the SMACS 0723 deep-field image - revealing thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky equivalent to a grain of sand held at arm's length - stopped me mid-scroll. I subsequently devoured every YouTube documentary and NASA press briefing I could find, gradually piecing together the staggering scope of what this 10-billion-dollar instrument was actually accomplishing.

What sets Webb apart, technically speaking, is its infrared capability. Whereas Hubble observes primarily in visible and ultraviolet wavelengths, Webb's segmented gold-coated mirror is optimised for infrared, enabling it to peer through cosmic dust clouds and observe light that has been redshifted from the universe's earliest epochs. In practical terms, this means we are now glimpsing galaxies as they appeared a mere few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

What fascinates me beyond the imagery itself is what Webb reveals about humanity. Here is an instrument representing thirty years of development, repeated budget overruns, and contributions from over fourteen countries - yet it works, sublimely. Were it not for international scientific collaboration of this calibre, such an achievement would be inconceivable.

solutions.text: PHẦN A — Viết lại câu (12 items)
Viết lại mỗi câu dưới đây dùng TỪ GỢI Ý (in hoa), giữ nguyên nghĩa và đúng dạng/collocation.
1. Astronomers believe that studying the (COSMOS) helps us understand our own origins as well as the origins of everything around us.
2. Some scientists speculate that (EXTRATERRESTRIAL) life could exist in environments we once assumed were entirely uninhabitable.
3. Many experts argue that any serious attempt to (COLONISE) another planet would require decades of preparation and international cooperation.
4. The surface of Mars is often described as (INHOSPITABLE) because of its thin atmosphere and extreme temperature swings.
5. Astronauts have to adapt quickly to (WEIGHTLESSNESS) once their spacecraft reaches orbit.
6. The cost of building and launching a new generation of space telescopes is widely considered (PROHIBITIVE) for most national space agencies acting alone.
7. Robotic (PROBE)s have been sent to explore the outer planets because sending humans there remains far beyond current technology.
8. Mission engineers must calculate a spacecraft's (TRAJECTORY) with extreme precision so that it reaches its intended destination.
9. Researchers are still debating how many exoplanets might actually be (HABITABLE) once we account for factors such as radiation and atmospheric composition.
10. The distances between stars are so vast that even our fastest spacecraft would take an (ASTRONOMICAL) amount of time to reach the nearest one.
11. Engineers continue to (GRAPPLE WITH) the challenge of shielding astronauts from cosmic radiation during long-duration missions.
12. The discovery of a new (EXOPLANET) orbiting a distant star often reignites public interest in the search for life beyond our solar system.

PHẦN A: 1. Astronomers believe that studying the cosmos helps us understand our own origins as well as the origins of everything around us. — "cosmos" luôn dùng ở số ít, chỉ vũ trụ như một tổng thể có trật tự; hay đi với "explore/study the cosmos". 2. Some scientists speculate that extraterrestrial life could exist in environments we once assumed were entirely uninhabitable. — tính từ "extraterrestrial" (ngoài Trái Đất) thường đi trước "life/beings"; phân biệt với "international". 3. Many experts argue that any serious attempt to colonise another planet would require decades of preparation and international cooperation. — chú ý chính tả Anh-Anh "colonise" (không phải "colonize"); hay đi với "colonise Mars/a planet". 4. The surface of Mars is often described as inhospitable because of its thin atmosphere and extreme temperature swings. — "inhospitable" mô tả môi trường khắc nghiệt, không phù hợp sinh sống; hay đi với "environment/conditions/climate". 5. Astronauts have to adapt quickly to weightlessness once their spacecraft reaches orbit. — danh từ chỉ trạng thái không trọng lượng; hay đi với "experience/a state of weightlessness". 6. The cost of building and launching a new generation of space telescopes is widely considered prohibitive for most national space agencies acting alone. — "prohibitive" (quá đắt đỏ, ngăn cản) khác với "prohibited" (bị cấm); hay đi với "prohibitive cost/price tag". 7. Robotic probes have been sent to explore the outer planets because sending humans there remains far beyond current technology. — danh từ "probe" chỉ tàu thăm dò không người lái; hay đi với "launch a probe/an interplanetary probe". 8. Mission engineers must calculate a spacecraft's trajectory with extreme precision so that it reaches its intended destination. — "trajectory" là đường bay/quỹ đạo của vật thể, khác với "orbit" (quỹ đạo khép kín quanh một thiên thể). 9. Researchers are still debating how many exoplanets might actually be habitable once we account for factors such as radiation and atmospheric composition. — "habitable" (có thể sống được) hay đi với "a habitable planet/zone"; trái nghĩa là "uninhabitable". 10. The distances between stars are so vast that even our fastest spacecraft would take an astronomical amount of time to reach the nearest one. — "astronomical" ở đây mang nghĩa "khổng lồ, khó tưởng tượng", khác với nghĩa gốc "thuộc thiên văn học". 11. Engineers continue to grapple with the challenge of shielding astronauts from cosmic radiation during long-duration missions. — cụm động từ luôn đi kèm giới từ "with", nghĩa là vật lộn/cố gắng giải quyết một vấn đề khó. 12. The discovery of a new exoplanet orbiting a distant star often reignites public interest in the search for life beyond our solar system. — "exoplanet" viết liền một từ, chỉ hành tinh ngoài hệ Mặt Trời.

PHẦN B: 1. Band 7: Although space exploration commands enormous budgets, it continues to be regarded as a worthwhile scientific investment. Band 8: Space exploration, notwithstanding its considerable price tag, is widely regarded as an investment whose scientific dividends far outweigh its costs. 2. Band 7: Astronauts must undergo years of rigorous training before they are cleared for a mission. Band 8: Rarely do astronauts set foot on a launch pad without having first endured years of gruelling physical and psychological preparation. 3. Band 7: Some experts believe that establishing a permanent base on the Moon should be a long-term priority. Band 8: It is the prospect of a permanent lunar base, rather than a fleeting visit, that many experts believe should anchor humanity's long-term space strategy. 4. Band 7: Private companies are increasingly taking on space missions that were once the exclusive domain of governments. Band 8: The growing privatisation of spaceflight means that private companies, rather than government agencies alone, now spearhead many of the most ambitious missions. 5. Band 7: Prolonged stays in space can pose serious risks to astronauts' physical health. Band 8: Were astronauts to remain in space for extended periods without adequate countermeasures, they would face serious risks ranging from bone density loss to radiation exposure. 6. Band 7: Scientists are eager to determine whether life exists on other planets, particularly those within a star's habitable zone. Band 8: Determining whether extraterrestrial life exists remains one of the most tantalising questions in modern astrobiology, particularly as habitable-zone exoplanets continue to be identified. 7. Band 6: Reusable rockets have made space travel cheaper. Band 8: So significant has the shift toward reusable rockets been that launch costs, once deemed prohibitive, are gradually falling within reach of a wider range of organisations. 8. Band 7: Space debris is increasingly seen as a serious threat to satellites and future missions. Band 8: There are growing concerns that, left unaddressed, the accumulation of space debris could trigger a Kessler-syndrome-style cascade, rendering entire orbital regions unusable.

The Commercialisation of Space: Space exploration is no longer the exclusive domain of governments (NASA, ESA). Private companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin have drastically reduced launch costs using reusable rockets.

Kessler Syndrome: A theoretical scenario where the density of space debris in low Earth orbit becomes so high that collisions create a cascading chain reaction, making future space exploration and satellite use impossible.

Model Answer (268 words):

The space mission that has captivated my imagination most profoundly is the James Webb Space Telescope - the long-awaited successor to Hubble, which was launched on Christmas Day 2021 and began returning its first full-colour scientific images in July 2022.

I first encountered Webb's imagery somewhat serendipitously while scrolling through Twitter that summer. The unveiling of the SMACS 0723 deep-field image - revealing thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky equivalent to a grain of sand held at arm's length - stopped me mid-scroll. I subsequently devoured every YouTube documentary and NASA press briefing I could find, gradually piecing together the staggering scope of what this 10-billion-dollar instrument was actually accomplishing.

What sets Webb apart, technically speaking, is its infrared capability. Whereas Hubble observes primarily in visible and ultraviolet wavelengths, Webb's segmented gold-coated mirror is optimised for infrared, enabling it to peer through cosmic dust clouds and observe light that has been redshifted from the universe's earliest epochs. In practical terms, this means we are now glimpsing galaxies as they appeared a mere few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

What fascinates me beyond the imagery itself is what Webb reveals about humanity. Here is an instrument representing thirty years of development, repeated budget overruns, and contributions from over fourteen countries - yet it works, sublimely. Were it not for international scientific collaboration of this calibre, such an achievement would be inconceivable.

For me, Webb embodies the noblest expression of human curiosity - a willingness to invest decades and billions simply to peer further into the dark, asking the most fundamental question of all: where did we come from?
Q1: Is space tourism ethically defensible?

P (Point): Space tourism, as currently practised, raises legitimate ethical concerns - particularly regarding its environmental footprint and its function as a status symbol for the ultra-wealthy - though dismissing it outright may overlook its longer-term potential to democratise space access.

E (Explain): The crux of the ethical debate lies in the disproportionate environmental cost relative to the social utility: a brief suborbital joyride emits as much carbon as an average person produces in a lifetime, while delivering little beyond personal gratification for paying customers.

E (Evidence): A peer-reviewed analysis in Earth's Future (Ryan et al., 2022) calculated that the soot emitted from rocket launches has a warming effect roughly 500 times more potent per unit mass than aircraft soot, with potential implications for stratospheric ozone if launch frequency continues to escalate. Additionally, a UCS report (Grego, 2023) documented that the number of objects launched into orbit tripled between 2018 and 2022, largely driven by commercial ventures.

L (Link): Consequently, while outright prohibition may be unrealistic, robust regulatory frameworks - including emissions caps and stratospheric impact assessments - are urgently needed before the industry's environmental externalities spiral out of control.
Q2: Should humanity seriously pursue the colonisation of Mars?

P (Point): While the colonisation of Mars makes for compelling science fiction, I find the proposition that it should rank among humanity's near-term priorities deeply questionable, given the scale of unresolved challenges here on Earth and the genuine inhospitability of the Martian environment.

E (Explain): Proponents frame Mars colonisation as a hedge against terrestrial catastrophe, but even the most degraded version of Earth would remain vastly more habitable than Mars, with its lethal radiation, atmospheric pressure incompatible with human physiology, and toxic perchlorate-laden soil.

E (Evidence): A study in GeoHealth (Zeitlin et al., 2013), based on data from NASA's Curiosity rover, estimated that astronauts on a round-trip Mars mission would absorb radiation doses approaching career limits set by NASA itself. Moreover, modelling published in Nature Astronomy (Jakosky et al., 2018) concluded that terraforming Mars with currently identifiable resources is essentially impossible - there simply isn't enough CO2 accessible to warm the planet sufficiently.

L (Link): Therefore, while scientific exploration of Mars remains entirely worthwhile, framing colonisation as a Plan B for humanity strikes me as a profound misallocation of intellectual and material resources.
Q3: How should the international community address the growing problem of space debris?

P (Point): Space debris represents one of the most pressing yet under-appreciated challenges of the spacefaring era, and tackling it effectively will require unprecedented international coordination, binding legal frameworks, and accelerated investment in active debris-removal technologies.

E (Explain): The fundamental issue is that low-Earth orbit operates as a commons - any single actor's debris jeopardises everyone's access - yet the existing international regulatory architecture, largely codified in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, was drafted long before commercial constellations existed.

E (Evidence): ESA's Annual Space Environment Report (2023) catalogued over 36,500 tracked debris objects larger than 10 centimetres, with millions of smaller untrackable fragments. A modelling study in Acta Astronautica (Liou & Johnson, 2008) and updated by subsequent analyses warned that even halting all launches today would not prevent the Kessler Syndrome - a cascading collision scenario - because existing debris will continue to generate fragments through mutual collisions.

L (Link): Accordingly, what's needed is a binding international treaty mandating debris-mitigation standards, end-of-life de-orbit requirements, and joint funding for active removal missions - lest we render entire orbital regions unusable for generations.

Lecture title: "Kessler's Cascade, the Habitability Index and the Mirage of Terraforming"
1. Section Type

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good afternoon. In our concluding lecture on space science, I want to puncture three pieces of received wisdom: that orbital space is effectively limitless, that habitability is a binary yes-or-no, and that terraforming is a serious near-term option. None of these claims survives scrutiny.

> Let's begin with Kessler syndrome, named for NASA scientist Donald Kessler, who in 1978 modelled a chilling scenario. As orbital debris accumulates — defunct satellites, spent boosters, fragments from anti-satellite tests — the probability of collision rises non-linearly. Each collision generates further fragments, which trigger further collisions, in a runaway cascade that could render whole orbital bands unusable for generations. The European Space Agency now tracks roughly thirty-six thousand objects larger than ten centimetres, and an estimated one million between one and ten centimetres — any of which travelling at orbital velocity can perforate a spacecraft.

> Now, habitability. The popular concept of the Goldilocks zone — neither too hot nor too cold — is a useful starting point but a poor finish. Modern astrobiologists employ a planetary habitability index that weights stellar stability, atmospheric retention, plate tectonics, magnetic shielding and biosignature potential. Out of roughly five thousand confirmed exoplanets, fewer than two dozen score even modestly on this composite. Habitability, in short, is multidimensional.

Now, I anticipate an objection brewing at the back of the room: surely, if low orbit becomes congested, we simply move higher? Well, that's where a counterintuitive bit of orbital mechanics bites. The most commercially coveted band — low Earth orbit, below two thousand kilometres — is also the one that self-cleans fastest, because residual atmospheric drag gradually de-orbits debris there over years or decades. Push your constellation up to medium or geostationary altitudes, and a defunct satellite can loiter for centuries, even millennia. [pause] So the tidy assumption that we can keep retreating upward actually trades a manageable problem for a near-permanent one.

Let me layer in a sobering economic dimension the headline figures tend to obscure. There's a concept the insurance industry has quietly adopted — the so-called orbital carrying capacity of a given altitude shell. Beyond a certain density of objects, the marginal collision risk imposed on every other operator rises steeply, yet no single company pays for the risk it externalises onto the commons. Economists will recognise this instantly as a tragedy-of-the-commons structure, transplanted four hundred kilometres above our heads. Um, and the mega-constellations now being launched — tens of thousands of satellites apiece — are, in effect, an uncontrolled experiment in that very capacity.

On habitability, I want to add one nuance that genuinely keeps astrobiologists up at night: the difference between a planet being habitable and being inhabited, and between either of those and being detectably so. Even if a world scored well on our composite index, a biosignature like atmospheric oxygen can, it turns out, be produced abiotically — by ultraviolet photolysis of water, for instance. [pause] So we may face false positives that no single telescope can resolve, requiring corroborating lines of evidence we don't yet possess. The upshot of all three threads — debris, habitability ambiguity, terraforming fantasy — is that our reach has outrun our stewardship. And that mismatch, ladies and gentlemen, is fundamentally a question not of physics but of governance, which is exactly where I want to take us next…

> Finally, terraforming Mars — beloved of billionaires and science-fiction writers alike. The physics is brutal. Mars has lost most of its atmosphere because it lacks a global magnetic field; any new atmosphere we manufactured would be stripped by solar wind within geological eyeblinks. Conservative estimates of the energy required exceed humanity's total annual production by orders of magnitude. It is not, in any meaningful sense, an engineering problem we can presently address. Right, turning to the policy implications…

•  Kham pha vu tru tao 'spin-off technologies' (vien thong ve tinh, chup anh y te) ma xa hoi nay coi la duong nhien.
•  Ve tinh quan trac Trai Dat thiet yeu de theo doi pha rung, nuoc bien dang, du bao bao — phan lon hieu biet ve khi hau den tu goc nhin quy dao.
•  Phong thu hanh tinh va dinh cu ngoai Trai Dat la 'bao hiem ton vong' truoc nguy co thien thach hay sieu nui lua.
Phia uu tien van de Trai Dat (Earth-first):
•  Cac su menh ton kem (vd: su menh Sao Hoa co nguoi lai uoc tinh tren mot nghin ti USD) co the tai tro tiem chung, giao duc hay cuu doi nhieu lan.
•  Co su kho chiu ve dao duc khi ty phu bay len rìa khong gian giai tri trong khi mot phan ba nhan loai thieu ve sinh co ban.
•  Tu goc nay, khong gian giong mot 'du an phu phiem' hon la mot bien gioi can chinh phuc.
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion
•  Introduction — dien giai tranh luan; luan diem: su danh doi giua khong gian va Trai Dat phan lon la gia tao vi hai dong ngan sach o quy mo hoan toan khac nhau.
•  Body 1 — phia uu tien khong gian: spin-off, ve tinh quan trac khi hau, phong thu hanh tinh nhu bao hiem ton vong.
•  Body 2 — phia uu tien Trai Dat: chi phi su menh khong lo doi lap nhu cau co ban, va su kho chiu dao duc voi du lich vu tru cua gioi sieu giau.
•  Conclusion — lap truong 'disaggregate the budget': dau tu vu tru o muc khiem ton va ben vung khong loai tru cuu tro nhan dao; tach bach hai dong la 'false economy'.
(5) Mẫu câu luyện tập (Practice sentences)

Cau phan bien phia Trai Dat

rows: "the long-term insurance value of becoming a multi-planetary species cannot be priced quarterly"
"sustained funding for fundamental research yields compounding, if delayed, returns"
"Earth-observation constellations now anchor real-time climate and disaster monitoring"
"We should focus on problems at home"
"terrestrial deprivation and space investment occupy entirely different fiscal scales"

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~259 words)

Whether humanity should pour resources into venturing beyond our atmosphere or concentrate first on terrestrial problems has become a perennial debate. Both camps make legitimate points, but in my view the dichotomy is overstated.

Champions of space exploration argue that pushing the cosmic frontier yields outsized scientific dividends. The Apollo programme, for example, produced spin-off technologies ranging from satellite communications to medical imaging that we now take for granted. Earth-observation satellites, in particular, are indispensable for tracking deforestation, monitoring sea-level rise and forecasting hurricanes — much of what we know about climate change comes from looking back from orbit. Furthermore, given that an asteroid impact could one day threaten our species, planetary defence and off-world colonisation are arguably insurance policies for civilisation.

Critics, however, contend that such missions are profligate when measured against unmet earthly needs. The cost of a single crewed Mars mission is estimated to exceed a trillion dollars, a sum which could fund universal vaccination, primary education or hunger relief many times over. There is also a moral discomfort in watching billionaires fly to the edge of space for leisure while millions lack reliable sanitation. From this angle, space looks less like a frontier and more like a vanity project.

In my view, the choice is not binary. The actual share of global GDP devoted to space agencies is under 0.1 per cent — hardly a drain that explains away poverty. Space exploration and humanitarian spending can, and arguably must, advance in parallel. A balanced budget, rather than an either/or stance, seems the most sensible position.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~275 words)

Few policy debates polarise public opinion as sharply as whether humanity should commit serious resources to space exploration or focus its energies on alleviating earthbound suffering. Although both perspectives are intellectually defensible, I am persuaded that the supposed trade-off is largely illusory.

Advocates of an expansive space agenda point to a cascade of tangible returns that often go unnoticed. The miniaturisation of electronics, advances in materials science and the entire architecture of global positioning — without which modern logistics and precision agriculture would falter — all owe a debt to public investment in aerospace. Earth-observation constellations, moreover, are now the linchpin of climate monitoring, supplying real-time data on Arctic ice loss and biosphere health. Seldom, indeed, has so small a fraction of GDP delivered such outsized civilisational dividends.

Sceptics, by contrast, frame planetary exploration as a misallocation of capital in a world still riddled with destitution. Why, they ask, dispatch probes to the outer solar system when hundreds of millions subsist on a few dollars a day? Compounding this critique is the rise of suborbital space tourism, whose carbon-intensive launches deliver scant scientific value while widening the optics gap between billionaire passengers and the global poor. Such concerns command genuine moral weight.

The reconciliation, in my view, lies in disaggregating the budget. Allocating modest yet sustained funding to fundamental research, planetary defence and Earth-observation missions need not crowd out development aid; the two streams operate on entirely different fiscal scales. Crucially, the long-term insurance value of becoming a multi-planetary species cannot be priced in quarterly terms. Decoupling space from humanitarian commitment is, ultimately, a false economy, and a pluralist stance is preferable to either extreme.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 mo bang nhan dinh sac ('the supposed trade-off is largely illusory') va dung dao ngu 'Seldom, indeed, has so small a fraction of GDP delivered...', trong khi Band 7 chi neu 'the dichotomy is overstated'.

•  Band 8 dung lexis Band 8 dac hon ('Earth-observation constellations', 'the linchpin of climate monitoring', 'optics gap', 'disaggregating the budget', 'a false economy', 'a multi-planetary species') va nominalisation ('the miniaturisation of electronics').

•  Band 8 lap luan 'tach bach ngan sach o quy mo tai khoa khac nhau' chat che hon va cohesion mach lac hon ('Compounding this critique is...', 'Crucially'), nang Task Response va Coherence ro ret so voi Band 7.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> What the James Webb Space Telescope has unveiled has fundamentally reshaped our understanding of the **cosmos**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Hy Lạp "kosmos" (trật tự, vẻ đẹp) → vũ trụ được nhìn như một chỉnh thể có trật tự.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Cosmos' luôn số ít; đừng nhầm với 'chaos' (hỗn loạn) dù hai từ trông có phần giống nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: the universe seen as a well-ordered, vast, and harmonious whole
vocabulary.definition_vi: vũ trụ (nhìn như một tổng thể có trật tự)
vocabulary.example: What the James Webb Space Telescope has unveiled has fundamentally reshaped our understanding of the cosmos.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Hy Lạp 'kosmos' (trật tự, vẻ đẹp) → vũ trụ được nhìn như một chỉnh thể có trật tự.

Cải tạo địa hình và khí quyển một hành tinh để giống Trái Đất, có thể sinh sống được.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Scientists propose using advanced technology to **terraform** Mars, making it Earth-like.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"terra" (đất, Trái Đất) + "form" (tạo hình) → biến một hành tinh khác thành giống Trái Đất.
vocabulary.common_error: Chỉ dùng cho hành tinh/thiên thể, không dùng cho việc cải tạo đất trên Trái Đất (dùng 'reclaim land' thay thế).
vocabulary.definition_en: to transform a planet's atmosphere and surface so as to resemble Earth, making it habitable for humans
vocabulary.definition_vi: cải tạo địa hình một hành tinh để giống Trái Đất, có thể sinh sống được
vocabulary.example: Scientists propose using advanced technology to terraform Mars, making it Earth-like.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'terra' (đất, Trái Đất) + 'form' (tạo hình) → biến một hành tinh khác thành giống Trái Đất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ngoài Trái Đất, ngoài hành tinh chúng ta.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Discovering **extraterrestrial** life remains one of the central priorities of modern astrobiology.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"extra-" (ngoài, vượt) + "terrestrial" (thuộc Trái Đất) → vượt ra ngoài Trái Đất.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường viết tắt là 'ET' trong văn nói; đừng nhầm 'extraterrestrial' (ngoài Trái Đất) với 'international' (quốc tế).
vocabulary.definition_en: originating, existing, or occurring outside the Earth or its atmosphere
vocabulary.definition_vi: ngoài Trái Đất, ngoài hành tinh
vocabulary.example: Discovering extraterrestrial life remains one of the central priorities of modern astrobiology.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'extra-' (ngoài, vượt) + 'terrestrial' (thuộc Trái Đất) → vượt ra ngoài Trái Đất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khai phá, thiết lập khu định cư trên một hành tinh hoặc vùng đất mới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It is far harder to **colonise** Mars than early lunar missions ever suggested, given the planet's harsh conditions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"colony" (thuộc địa, khu định cư) → colonise = lập nên một khu định cư mới.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh là '-ise' (colonise), không phải '-ize' (colonize) như tiếng Anh-Mỹ.
vocabulary.definition_en: to send settlers to and establish political and social control over an area, planet, or territory
vocabulary.definition_vi: khai phá, thiết lập khu định cư (trên một hành tinh)
vocabulary.example: It is far harder to colonise Mars than early lunar missions ever suggested, given the planet's harsh conditions.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'colony' (thuộc địa, khu định cư) → colonise = lập nên một khu định cư mới.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khắc nghiệt, không phù hợp để sinh sống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The Martian surface is incredibly **inhospitable**, featuring toxic soil and an unbreathable atmosphere.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"in-" (không) + "hospitable" (hiếu khách, dễ chịu) → môi trường không "chào đón" sự sống.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'inhospitable' (khắc nghiệt, môi trường) với 'inhospitable' dùng cho người thiếu hiếu khách — nghĩa vẫn liên quan nhưng ngữ cảnh khoa học tự nhiên khác với xã giao.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of an environment) harsh and difficult to live in; not welcoming or comfortable
vocabulary.definition_vi: khắc nghiệt, không phù hợp để sinh sống
vocabulary.example: The Martian surface is incredibly inhospitable, featuring toxic soil and an unbreathable atmosphere.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'in-' (không) + 'hospitable' (hiếu khách, dễ chịu) → môi trường không 'chào đón' sự sống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trạng thái không trọng lượng, như các phi hành gia trải nghiệm trong quỹ đạo.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Astronauts suffer significant bone density loss caused by months of **weightlessness** during deep space travel.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"weight" (trọng lượng) + "-less" (không có) + "-ness" (trạng thái) → trạng thái như không có trọng lượng.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm với 'zero gravity' — về mặt vật lý vẫn có trọng lực, nhưng vật thể trong quỹ đạo rơi tự do liên tục nên cảm thấy 'không trọng lượng'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the condition of experiencing no apparent gravitational pull, as astronauts do in orbit
vocabulary.definition_vi: trạng thái không trọng lượng (trong không gian)
vocabulary.example: Astronauts suffer significant bone density loss caused by months of weightlessness during deep space travel.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'weight' (trọng lượng) + '-less' (không có) + '-ness' (trạng thái) → trạng thái như không có trọng lượng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá đắt đỏ, mức chi phí ngăn cản việc thực hiện.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The funding required for a crewed Mars mission is **prohibitive**, demanding cooperation between governments and private billionaires.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"prohibit" (cấm, ngăn cản) → "prohibitive" cost = chi phí cao đến mức "ngăn cản" người ta mua.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'prohibitive' (quá đắt, cản trở) với 'prohibited' (bị cấm) — hai từ có nghĩa khác nhau dù cùng gốc.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a cost or price) excessively high, so as to prevent the use or purchase of something
vocabulary.definition_vi: quá đắt đỏ, ngăn cản việc thực hiện (chi phí)
vocabulary.example: The funding required for a crewed Mars mission is prohibitive, demanding cooperation between governments and private billionaires.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'prohibit' (cấm, ngăn cản) → 'prohibitive' cost = chi phí cao đến mức 'ngăn cản' người ta mua.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Gây kinh ngạc, choáng ngợp với cảm giác cảm phục sâu sắc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Witnessing a human walk on another planet would be an absolutely **awe-inspiring** achievement.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"awe" (sự kinh ngạc, cảm phục) + "inspiring" (truyền cảm hứng) → khiến người ta vừa kinh ngạc vừa cảm phục.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn có gạch nối 'awe-inspiring' khi dùng làm tính từ ghép trước danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: causing feelings of profound respect, wonder, or admiration
vocabulary.definition_vi: gây kinh ngạc, choáng ngợp (đầy cảm phục)
vocabulary.example: Witnessing a human walk on another planet would be an absolutely awe-inspiring achievement.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'awe' (sự kinh ngạc, cảm phục) + 'inspiring' (truyền cảm hứng) → khiến người ta vừa kinh ngạc vừa cảm phục.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tàu thăm dò không người lái được gửi đi thu thập thông tin về thiên thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The space **probe** transmitted stunning close-up images of Jupiter's moons back to Earth.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tàu "probe" (thăm dò) đi "dò" những vùng con người chưa từng đặt chân tới.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Probe' cũng là động từ nghĩa 'điều tra sâu' trong ngữ cảnh khác; ở đây chỉ dùng danh từ nghĩa thiết bị không gian.
vocabulary.definition_en: an unmanned spacecraft sent to gather and transmit information about a distant celestial body
vocabulary.definition_vi: tàu thăm dò (không người lái)
vocabulary.example: The space probe transmitted stunning close-up images of Jupiter's moons back to Earth.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tàu 'probe' (thăm dò) đi 'dò' những vùng con người chưa từng đặt chân tới.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự tư nhân hoá, chuyển giao từ nhà nước sang tư nhân quản lý.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **privatisation** of spaceflight has driven down launch costs dramatically over the past decade.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"private" (tư nhân) + "-isation" (quá trình chuyển đổi) → chuyển từ nhà nước sang tư nhân quản lý.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh dùng '-isation' (privatisation), tiếng Mỹ dùng '-ization' (privatization).
vocabulary.definition_en: the transfer of an industry or service from public/government control to private ownership or management
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tư nhân hoá
vocabulary.example: The privatisation of spaceflight has driven down launch costs dramatically over the past decade.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'private' (tư nhân) + '-isation' (quá trình chuyển đổi) → chuyển từ nhà nước sang tư nhân quản lý.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quỹ đạo bay, đường đi cong của vật thể trong không gian.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Mission controllers had to make precise adjustments to keep the spacecraft's **trajectory** on course.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin "trans-" (qua) + "jacere" (ném) → đường đi của vật bị "ném" xuyên qua không gian.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'trajectory' (quỹ đạo bay của vật thể) với 'orbit' (quỹ đạo quay quanh một thiên thể) — trajectory rộng hơn, có thể không khép kín.
vocabulary.definition_en: the curved path followed by an object moving through space, such as a spacecraft or projectile
vocabulary.definition_vi: quỹ đạo bay, đường đi (của tàu vũ trụ)
vocabulary.example: Mission controllers had to make precise adjustments to keep the spacecraft's trajectory on course.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Latin 'trans-' (qua) + 'jacere' (ném) → đường đi của vật bị 'ném' xuyên qua không gian.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có thể sống được, phù hợp để sinh sống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Fewer than two dozen of the thousands of confirmed exoplanets score even modestly on the **habitability** index.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"habitat" (môi trường sống) + "-able" (có thể) → nơi có thể trở thành môi trường sống.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'habitable' (có thể sống được) với 'inhabitable' — thực chất cả hai từ đều mang nghĩa 'có thể ở được', trong khi 'uninhabitable' mới là 'không thể ở được'.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a planet or environment) suitable for people, animals, or plants to live in
vocabulary.definition_vi: có thể sống được, phù hợp để sinh sống
vocabulary.example: Fewer than two dozen of the thousands of confirmed exoplanets score even modestly on the habitability index.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'habitat' (môi trường sống) + '-able' (có thể) → nơi có thể trở thành môi trường sống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khổng lồ, khủng khiếp về số lượng; hoặc thuộc về thiên văn học.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The cost of a crewed Mars mission is **astronomical**, running into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Con số lớn như khoảng cách giữa các vì sao ("astronomy") → "astronomical" = lớn đến mức không tưởng.
vocabulary.common_error: Nghĩa 'khổng lồ' (informal, dùng cho số tiền/chi phí) khác với nghĩa gốc 'thuộc thiên văn học' (formal, khoa học) — cần phân biệt theo ngữ cảnh.
vocabulary.definition_en: extremely large in amount or scale; also, relating to the scientific study of stars and planets
vocabulary.definition_vi: khổng lồ, khủng khiếp (số lượng); hoặc thuộc thiên văn học
vocabulary.example: The cost of a crewed Mars mission is astronomical, running into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Con số lớn như khoảng cách giữa các vì sao ('astronomy') → 'astronomical' = lớn đến mức không tưởng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vật lộn, cố gắng giải quyết một vấn đề khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Engineers continue to **grapple with** the challenge of protecting astronauts from cosmic radiation on long missions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"grapple" (móc, vật lộn tay đôi) + "with" → như đang vật lộn trực tiếp với một vấn đề khó.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn đi kèm giới từ 'with'; không dùng 'grapple to' hay 'grapple against'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try hard to deal with or understand a difficult problem or challenge
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn, cố gắng giải quyết (một vấn đề khó)
vocabulary.example: Engineers continue to grapple with the challenge of protecting astronauts from cosmic radiation on long missions.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grapple' (móc, vật lộn tay đôi) + 'with' → như đang vật lộn trực tiếp với một vấn đề khó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dần được ủng hộ rộng rãi, ngày càng được chú ý.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The idea of asteroid mining has **gained significant traction** among private aerospace companies in recent years.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Bánh xe cần "traction" (độ bám đường) để lăn đi → ý tưởng cần được "bám" vào sự ủng hộ để lan rộng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Traction' vốn có nghĩa vật lý là 'lực kéo/độ bám'; trong nghĩa bóng luôn đi với động từ 'gain' hoặc 'lose', không dùng 'have'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to gradually gain acceptance, support, or popularity
vocabulary.definition_vi: dần được ủng hộ rộng rãi, ngày càng được chú ý
vocabulary.example: The idea of asteroid mining has gained significant traction among private aerospace companies in recent years.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Bánh xe cần 'traction' (độ bám đường) để lăn đi → ý tưởng cần được 'bám' vào sự ủng hộ để lan rộng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Rác vũ trụ, các mảnh vỡ vệ tinh và tên lửa cũ trôi nổi quanh quỹ đạo Trái Đất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Orbital **debris** poses a significant threat to functioning satellites and the International Space Station.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"space" (không gian) + "debris" (mảnh vỡ) → những mảnh rác trôi nổi ngoài quỹ đạo Trái Đất.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Debris' là danh từ không đếm được và chữ 's' cuối không phát âm rõ trong tiếng Anh chuẩn (/ˈdeb.riː/), không phải /dɪˈbriːz/.
vocabulary.definition_en: defunct man-made objects in orbit around Earth, such as old satellites and rocket fragments, that pose a collision risk
vocabulary.definition_vi: rác vũ trụ (mảnh vỡ vệ tinh, tên lửa cũ)
vocabulary.example: Orbital debris poses a significant threat to functioning satellites and the International Space Station.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'space' (không gian) + 'debris' (mảnh vỡ) → những mảnh rác trôi nổi ngoài quỹ đạo Trái Đất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hội chứng Kessler, chuỗi va chạm rác vũ trụ mất kiểm soát trong quỹ đạo thấp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The runaway collisional cascade known as **Kessler syndrome** was first modelled by NASA scientist Donald Kessler in 1978.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Đặt theo tên nhà khoa học Donald Kessler → chuỗi phản ứng va chạm rác vũ trụ tự nhân lên như hiệu ứng domino.
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là danh từ riêng, luôn viết hoa chữ 'Kessler'; không nhầm với 'syndrome' dùng trong y học thông thường.
vocabulary.definition_en: a theoretical scenario in which the density of objects in low Earth orbit is high enough to cause a runaway cascade of collisions
vocabulary.definition_vi: hội chứng Kessler (chuỗi va chạm rác vũ trụ mất kiểm soát)
vocabulary.example: The runaway collisional cascade known as Kessler syndrome was first modelled by NASA scientist Donald Kessler in 1978.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Đặt theo tên nhà khoa học Donald Kessler → chuỗi phản ứng va chạm rác vũ trụ tự nhân lên như hiệu ứng domino.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chỉ số khả năng sinh sống, đo mức độ một hành tinh phù hợp cho sự sống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Fewer than two dozen of the roughly five thousand confirmed exoplanets score even modestly on the composite **habitability index**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"habitability" (khả năng sống được) + "index" (chỉ số) → thước đo tổng hợp mức độ một hành tinh có thể ở được.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Index' số nhiều học thuật là 'indices', không phải 'indexes', trong văn phong khoa học trang trọng.
vocabulary.definition_en: a composite scientific measure used to rate how suitable a planet is for supporting life
vocabulary.definition_vi: chỉ số khả năng sinh sống (đo mức độ một hành tinh phù hợp cho sự sống)
vocabulary.example: Fewer than two dozen of the roughly five thousand confirmed exoplanets score even modestly on the composite habitability index.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'habitability' (khả năng sống được) + 'index' (chỉ số) → thước đo tổng hợp mức độ một hành tinh có thể ở được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vùng Goldilocks, khu vực quanh một ngôi sao có nhiệt độ vừa phải để tồn tại nước lỏng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Orbiting within the **Goldilocks zone** is a useful starting point but a poor finish for assessing planetary habitability.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Từ chuyện "Goldilocks" chọn cháo "vừa đủ nóng, không quá nóng không quá lạnh" → vùng có nhiệt độ "vừa đủ" cho sự sống.
collocations: the Goldilocks zone of a star
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn viết hoa 'Goldilocks' vì bắt nguồn từ tên nhân vật truyện cổ tích; không dùng số nhiều 'zones' khi nói về một hệ sao cụ thể.
vocabulary.definition_en: the region around a star where conditions are just right for liquid water to exist on a planet's surface
vocabulary.definition_vi: vùng Goldilocks (vùng có nhiệt độ vừa phải để tồn tại nước lỏng)
vocabulary.example: Orbiting within the Goldilocks zone is a useful starting point but a poor finish for assessing planetary habitability.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Từ chuyện 'Goldilocks' chọn cháo 'vừa đủ nóng, không quá nóng không quá lạnh' → vùng có nhiệt độ 'vừa đủ' cho sự sống.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hành tinh ngoài hệ Mặt Trời, quay quanh một ngôi sao khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The discovery of **exoplanets**, now numbering in the thousands, has profoundly recalibrated our understanding of the cosmos.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"exo-" (bên ngoài) + "planet" (hành tinh) → hành tinh nằm ngoài hệ Mặt Trời của chúng ta.
vocabulary.common_error: Không viết cách 'exo planet'; luôn viết liền một từ 'exoplanet'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a planet that orbits a star outside our solar system
vocabulary.definition_vi: hành tinh ngoài hệ Mặt Trời
vocabulary.example: The discovery of exoplanets, now numbering in the thousands, has profoundly recalibrated our understanding of the cosmos.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'exo-' (bên ngoài) + 'planet' (hành tinh) → hành tinh nằm ngoài hệ Mặt Trời của chúng ta.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiếm khi, rất ít khi xảy ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Since he moved to another country, I only get to see him **once in a blue moon**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Trăng xanh ("blue moon") là hiện tượng thiên văn hiếm gặp → việc xảy ra "once in a blue moon" cũng hiếm như vậy.
collocations: happen once in a blue moon
visit once in a blue moon
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ cố định, không đổi 'moon' thành số nhiều hay thêm tính từ khác vào giữa cụm.
vocabulary.definition_en: very rarely; almost never
vocabulary.definition_vi: hiếm khi, rất ít khi xảy ra
vocabulary.example: Since he moved to another country, I only get to see him once in a blue moon.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Trăng xanh ('blue moon') là hiện tượng thiên văn hiếm gặp → việc xảy ra 'once in a blue moon' cũng hiếm như vậy.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vươn tới những ước mơ lớn lao, đầy tham vọng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> My parents always encouraged me to **reach for the stars** and pursue my biggest dreams.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Các vì sao ("stars") ở rất xa, khó chạm tới → "reach for the stars" = theo đuổi ước mơ lớn, khó đạt được.
collocations: encourage sb to reach for the stars
dare to reach for the stars
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ mang tính ẩn dụ, không dùng theo nghĩa đen về việc bay lên vũ trụ thật sự.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be extremely ambitious and aim for something very difficult to achieve
vocabulary.definition_vi: vươn tới những ước mơ lớn lao, đầy tham vọng
vocabulary.example: My parents always encouraged me to reach for the stars and pursue my biggest dreams.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Các vì sao ('stars') ở rất xa, khó chạm tới → 'reach for the stars' = theo đuổi ước mơ lớn, khó đạt được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Không phải chuyện khó hiểu hay khó làm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Come on, fixing this simple computer glitch is **not rocket science**!

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Khoa học tên lửa ("rocket science") vốn nổi tiếng là phức tạp → nói điều gì đó "not rocket science" nghĩa là nó đơn giản hơn nhiều.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng ở dạng phủ định 'not rocket science'; câu khẳng định 'it's rocket science' nghe kỳ lạ trừ khi cố ý mỉa mai.
vocabulary.definition_en: used to say that something is not difficult to understand or do
vocabulary.definition_vi: không phải chuyện khó hiểu/khó làm
vocabulary.example: Come on, fixing this simple computer glitch is not rocket science!
vocabulary.memory_hook: Khoa học tên lửa ('rocket science') vốn nổi tiếng là phức tạp → nói điều gì đó 'not rocket science' nghĩa là nó đơn giản hơn nhiều.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nhật thực, hiện tượng Mặt Trăng che khuất ánh sáng Mặt Trời.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A total **solar eclipse** is a spectacular and rare astronomical event that draws crowds worldwide.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"solar" (thuộc Mặt Trời) + "eclipse" (che khuất) → Mặt Trời bị Mặt Trăng che khuất.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'solar eclipse' (nhật thực, mặt trăng che mặt trời) với 'lunar eclipse' (nguyệt thực, Trái Đất che mặt trăng).
vocabulary.definition_en: an astronomical event in which the moon passes between the sun and Earth, blocking some or all of the sun's light
vocabulary.definition_vi: nhật thực
vocabulary.example: A total solar eclipse is a spectacular and rare astronomical event that draws crowds worldwide.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'solar' (thuộc Mặt Trời) + 'eclipse' (che khuất) → Mặt Trời bị Mặt Trăng che khuất.
